text:
B: Hi! Can you hear me alright? I'm Luke.
A: Hello, love, yes, I can hear you lovely. I'm Debbie. Sorry, I've got my glasses right on the end of my nose, I can't see the screen otherwise.
B: Ha, no, you're fine. Where are you calling from?
A: Gorleston. That's just by Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, you know, right on the coast.
B: Oh, lovely, by the sea. I'm in Bristol. Horfield, up the north side.
A: Bristol, ooh. I've never been, I don't think. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start?
B: I did, yeah. I was quite pleased with myself, actually. I think I sort of got into a rhythm with it. How did you get on?
A: Erm, I got about halfway and then Tilly, that's my dog, started barking at the postman, and that was me done, I lost my place completely. So I don't know what I've put, love, honestly.
B: That's fair. Postman's a legitimate distraction.
A: That is, that is. Here, I saw your photo, that little drawing of a dog on your shelf. Did one of yours do that?
B: Yeah, that's my daughter, Isla. She's nine. She's desperate for a dog, so she draws them instead, kind of as a hint. It's not working yet.
A: Oh bless her. My grandson's four and it's all diggers with him. Diggers, diggers, diggers. He's with me three days a week, and if we go along the seafront and there's roadworks, well, that's the morning gone, we're stood there watching the man in the digger for an hour. Sorry, I've gone off on one, what was I saying?
B: No, I love that. Honestly that's a pretty good morning out.
A: Free entertainment, innit. Better than the car park, they've put the charges up again.
B: Oh, don't. So are you working, or is it mostly grandson duty?
A: Mostly him now, really. I was on the packing line at a frozen food place near Yarmouth for years, and then they changed the shifts round and I couldn't do it with minding him, so I just sort of... stopped. Two years ago now. I keep saying I'll do a few hours at a charity shop, but I never get round to it, do you know what I mean?
B: Yeah, totally. I'm an executive assistant, so I basically run the managing director's diary at an engineering consultancy. Meetings, travel, board stuff, keeping the right people in front of him and the wrong ones away. It sounds dull, but you end up knowing everything that's going on, which I sort of secretly enjoy.
A: Ooh, you're the one in charge really, then.
B: Don't tell him that. But, yeah, a bit.
A: My husband Steve's self-employed, he does removals with his van, so there's no diary with him. He just answers the phone and goes. Mind you, the van's just failed its MOT, so he's not going anywhere this week.
B: Oh no. That's a pain when it's your living.
A: That is. What do you do when you're not working, then, love?
B: Erm, films, mostly. There's a cinema here called the Watershed that does foreign stuff, so I saw a Korean film there last week, which was gorgeous, sort of slow and sad. And I cook a lot. I make my own kimchi, though the last batch went a bit wrong. The whole kitchen smelled of it.
A: Kimchi! I wouldn't know where to start. I'm more of a shepherd's pie girl. And musicals. I've seen Mamma Mia twice, and we do the panto at the Pavilion every year with the grandkids.
B: Oh, panto's brilliant, though. I took Isla to the Hippodrome one a couple of years ago and she shouted herself hoarse.
A: That's the best bit, isn't it, the shouting. Oh, he's behind you!
B: Exactly. Did you ever think about going on holiday to-
